blurb: Why robots lag chatbots, robot foundation models, self-driving cars and the humanoid push.

cards.title: The physical world bites back

steps.p: What is hard for people, like chess, can be easy for computers. What is easy for a toddler, like picking up a sock, is extremely hard for robots.
Language models learned from trillions of words online. There is no comparable trove of recorded robot movements.
A wrong word costs nothing; a wrong move breaks things or hurts people, so learning by trial and error is slow and risky.

cards.aside: Robotics is often described as being where language AI was around 2018 or 2019.

options: High-level reasoning is relatively easy for machines, while basic perception and movement are hard
cards.why: Easy for us is hard for them. Evolution spent hundreds of millions of years refining perception and movement, so they feel effortless to us but hide enormous complexity.

cards.statement: Robotics has an internet-scale dataset of robot actions, comparable to the text that trains language models.
cards.why: False. Robot data must be collected on physical hardware, slowly. That shortage is one of the field's central bottlenecks.

cards.q: A common way to gather robot training data is…
options: Teleoperation: humans remotely control robots to demonstrate tasks
cards.why: Teleoperation. Operators perform tasks through the robot itself, recording exactly the sensor readings and motor commands a learned policy needs.

cards.title: In 2023, 21 institutions pooled their robot data into one dataset spanning 22 different robot types.
cards.detail: The Open X-Embodiment project, led by Google DeepMind, gathered over a million robot episodes, and found models trained on the mix often beat those trained on a single robot's data.

cards.statement: A robot trained in one lab kitchen often struggles when moved to a different kitchen.
cards.why: True. New lighting, layouts and objects throw off policies trained in narrow settings. Generalizing to new homes is a major goal.

cards.title: Vision-language-action models

steps.p: Take a model pretrained on web images and text, which already knows what a mug or a banana is.
Fine-tune it on robot data to output motor commands, so its inputs are camera images plus an instruction.
Web knowledge helps the robot handle objects and instructions never seen in its own training data.

cards.aside: Google DeepMind's RT-2 (2023) and Physical Intelligence's π0 (2024) are prominent examples.

options: Robot actions, such as arm movements and gripper commands
cards.why: Actions. Some encode actions as tokens like words; others generate continuous motor trajectories.

cards.statement: RT-2 could follow instructions involving concepts absent from its robot training data, thanks to web pretraining.
cards.why: True. For example, it could place an object next to a picture of a specific celebrity, recognizing them from web knowledge rather than robot demonstrations.

options: Predicts a short sequence of future actions at once, giving smoother motion
cards.why: Planning a few moves ahead. Predicting chunks reduces jittery step-by-step corrections and compounding errors.

cards.title: Physical Intelligence's π0 model folded laundry taken straight from a hamper.
cards.detail: Laundry is notoriously hard for robots: cloth has endless possible shapes. The 2024 demo was seen as a milestone for general-purpose manipulation.

cards.q: Why are soft things like clothes especially hard for robots?
options: They can take endless shapes and are hard to model or simulate
They are slippery only when wet
cards.why: Infinite configurations. A rigid cup has six degrees of freedom. A shirt effectively has thousands, and its behavior is hard to predict.

cards.title: How a robotaxi drives

steps.p: Cameras, lidar and radar build a 3D picture of the surroundings, detecting cars, people and signs.
The system forecasts what everyone nearby is likely to do over the next few seconds.
It chooses a safe, comfortable path and speed, updating many times a second.

cards.aside: Waymo operates fully driverless paid rides in several US cities.

options: Timing how long laser pulses take to bounce back
cards.why: Laser time-of-flight. Millions of pulses per second produce a precise 3D point cloud, even in darkness.

options: Can drive with no human driver within a defined area and conditions
Can drive anywhere in any condition
cards.why: Driverless within limits. Level 4 robotaxis operate without a driver inside a mapped service area. Level 5 — anywhere, anytime — does not yet exist.

cards.title: In the 2004 DARPA Grand Challenge, no self-driving car finished — the best managed about 7 miles of a 150-mile desert course.
cards.detail: A year later, five vehicles finished, led by Stanford's Stanley. Many of the engineers involved went on to found the self-driving industry.

cards.statement: Tesla's standard Autopilot is a Level 4 system that requires no driver attention.
cards.why: False. Autopilot and Tesla's supervised self-driving features are driver-assistance systems requiring an attentive driver ready to take over.

cards.statement: Waymo operates fully driverless, paid robotaxi rides in multiple US cities.
cards.why: True. Including Phoenix, San Francisco and Los Angeles, with no safety driver on board.

cards.title: Why build robots shaped like us?

steps.p: Stairs, doors, tools and workstations are designed for human bodies. A human-shaped robot could use them without changes.
Human video and teleoperation map more naturally onto a similar body.
Dexterous hands, battery life, safety around people and cost are all still major challenges.

cards.aside: Companies including Figure, Tesla, Agility, Unitree, Boston Dynamics and 1X are all building humanoids.

cards.q: The main argument for making general-purpose robots humanoid is…
options: Our environments and tools are designed for human bodies
Two legs are faster than wheels
cards.why: Compatibility. A humanoid could, in principle, step into any human job without redesigning the workplace. Skeptics argue wheels and simpler arms are more practical for most tasks.

cards.statement: Boston Dynamics retired its hydraulic Atlas robot and unveiled an all-electric version in 2024.
cards.why: True. The electric Atlas, announced in April 2024, is aimed at commercial work, starting with Hyundai's factories.

cards.q: What is often called the hardest part of a humanoid to get right?
options: Dexterous hands with fine control and touch sensing
cards.why: Hands. A human hand has over 20 degrees of freedom and rich touch sensing. Matching that reliably and cheaply remains unsolved.

cards.title: Chinese maker Unitree priced its G1 humanoid from about $16,000 in 2024.
cards.detail: That was a fraction of earlier humanoids' cost, reflecting China's strong position in robot hardware and components.

cards.title: Watch robot demos like a skeptic
cards.body: Many impressive robot videos are teleoperated, sped up or the best of many attempts. Good demos say so in the caption.
cards.challenge: Next time you see a robot video, look for "autonomous", "teleoperated" or a speed label like "2×" before being impressed.
